finding.claim: Mass assignment on PUT /me: the entire request body is merged into the authenticated user object and persisted, so a user can set privileged or protected fields (e.g. role, isAdmin, id, email verification status, or other users' ownership fields) and escalate privileges or tamper with account state. The response also returns the full user object. Impact depends on the user schema, which is not in this directory.
finding.source: req.body (JSON) from any authenticated user on PUT /me

trace.note: PUT /me handler; no field allowlist or validation
Object.assign copies all attacker-supplied keys onto req.user

finding.guards_checked: No allowlist, schema validation, or role check in this file. The auth middleware that sets req.user is not in the directory, so it cannot be confirmed. Even if it exists, it does not limit which fields can be written. The sibling route at line 10 destructures only displayName and bio, which shows the intended allowlist pattern and that /me lacks it. Object.assign does not set the prototype through a __proto__ key, so prototype pollution is not claimed.

verdict.reason: users.js:5 does Object.assign(req.user, req.body) with no allowlist, users.js:6 persists it, and users.js:7 returns it, while the sibling route at users.js:11-12 destructures only displayName and bio. Any authenticated user can reach this, and nothing in the directory blocks it. The actual impact depends on the user schema and on the auth middleware, neither of which is in this directory.
